column4: This ayah gathers the section's whole emotional arc: لَا تَجِدُ introduces a finding, affection is bounded by its proper object, faith is set in hearts, and رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ makes satisfaction reciprocal.

The response to distribution is stated in the section's exact sequence and opposition: when they are given they are pleased, and when they are not given they become angry; أُعْطُوا ... رَضُوا and يَسْخَطُونَ expose a corrupt version of gift producing satisfaction.

This supplies the rightly directed alternative to 9:58: being content with what Allah and His messenger give would turn reception into trust and desire toward Allah, precisely the gift-to-rida movement of فَتَرْضَىٰ.
This is the Quran's other use of the q-l-y root, and Lot's لِعَمَلِكُم مِّنَ الْقَالِينَ directs loathing explicitly at his people's acts rather than leaving its object as a person.

Allah makes faith beloved and beautifies it in hearts while making disbelief, defiance, and disobedience hateful; it is the clearest parallel to feelings being placed in the heart and aimed at their proper objects.
Allah casts مَحَبَّةً مِّنِّي upon the exposed infant Moses; divinely placed love is the direct opposite pole to the hatred denied in 93:3, and it causes others to receive the vulnerable child.
Allah sees the Prophet repeatedly turning his face skyward and turns him toward قِبْلَةً تَرْضَاهَا; an observed orientation is answered by a gift of direction that pleases him.

The Prophet is told to endure speech and glorify through the night's hours and the day's edges لَعَلَّكَ تَرْضَىٰ, making satisfaction an attained result across alternating times rather than an instantaneous feeling.
وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ repeats the promise structure of 93:5 almost word for word, but promises satisfaction to the self-purifying giver described in the preceding ayat.

The arrangement is said to be likelier to cool the wives' eyes, keep them from grieving, and make all of them satisfied with what the Prophet gives them; gift, grief's removal, and rida are joined in one relational scene.
رَاضِيَةً مَّرْضِيَّةً depicts the soul returning to its Lord both satisfied and approved, joining heartward return with the two-sided rida developed in the section.
رَّضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ names divine-human satisfaction in both directions, the Quranic realization of the section's mutual form of rida.
After truthfulness receives its lasting reward, رَّضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ makes mutual satisfaction the relation between the giver of the gardens and their recipients.
Allah's satisfaction with the first believers and their satisfaction with Him accompany prepared gardens, so reciprocal rida and a divine gift are explicitly bound together.
Parents may decide weaning عَن تَرَاضٍ مِّنْهُمَا وَتَشَاوُرٍ; this is literal two-party satisfaction governing care for a dependent child and excluding unilateral force.
The ban on consuming one another's property permits trade only عَن تَرَاضٍ مِّنكُمْ, directly clarifying the section's move from qahr as taking without consent to rida as the condition for taking.
Allah places compassion and mercy in the hearts of Jesus's followers; this parallels the source dictionary's āwā as a heart turning toward another and becoming tender.
Allah may place affection between the believers and those they have treated as enemies, making a divinely caused turn from hostility to love visible.
Allah places affection and mercy between spouses so that each finds repose with the other; the emotion is bestowed, relational, and reciprocal rather than merely private.
Abraham asks Allah to make people's hearts incline toward his vulnerable family and provide them fruits so they may be grateful; heartward turning and provision are joined as cause and response.

Allah reminds an exposed, fearful community that He sheltered them, strengthened them, and gave good provision so they might be grateful; فَآوَاكُمْ expands the orphan's shelter into communal divine care.
Joseph takes his brother into his own lodging with آوَىٰ إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ and immediately tells him not to grieve, bringing refuge, familial love, and grief's easing into one act.
The youths are told to take refuge in the cave, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease for them; physical shelter becomes the site of tender divine provision.
Pharaoh's wife calls the found infant a comfort of the eye, forbids his killing, and hopes to adopt him; this shows the love cast on Moses in 20:39 turning a heart toward protecting him.

This continuation of 20:39 returns Moses to his mother so that her eye may be cooled and she may not grieve, then recalls his rescue from distress; bestowed love culminates in relieved sorrow and care.
Moses is returned to his mother so her eye may be cooled and she may not grieve, making emotional restoration the outcome of the infant's divinely managed refuge.

لَتَجِدَنَّ frames a finding about emotional direction: some people are found most intense in enmity while others are nearest in affection, allowing the w-j-d root to carry sharply opposed heart-relations.

Those unable to join turn away with eyes overflowing in grief because they cannot find anything to spend; يَجِدُونَ and حَزَنًا occur together, explicitly joining the root's ordinary 'find' sense to its dictionary face of grief.

True submission requires that people find no inner resistance to the Prophet's judgment; لَا يَجِدُوا فِي أَنفُسِهِمْ حَرَجًا makes finding an inward state and distinguishes willing acceptance from coerced compliance.
The hosts find no need or resentment in their breasts concerning what the emigrants are given and prefer them over themselves; an inward finding, another's gift, and generous affection converge.
Allah is pleased with the believers, knows what is in their hearts, and sends tranquility and a near victory; divine rida, the heart's state, and subsequent giving form one causal sequence.
Former enemies become brothers when Allah joins their hearts and rescues them from a brink; this is a divinely effected reversal in the direction of human feeling.
Allah joins the believers' hearts in a way no expenditure of all earthly wealth could have achieved, showing the heart's turn as a divine gift beyond human effort or payment.
Divine mercy makes the Prophet gentle; hardness of heart would scatter people, while pardon and consultation enact the tender turn toward them that the āwā dictionary sense describes.

Those who love that Allah forgive them are told to pardon and overlook needy kin; hoped-for divine favor is converted into merciful treatment of a vulnerable other, as satisfaction in the section becomes care for the orphan.
The command to give orphans their property and never consume it into one's own directly specifies what refusing to overpower an orphan means in material dealings.
Guardians must test orphans, deliver their wealth at maturity, avoid consuming it wastefully, and call witnesses; the ayah turns non-coercive care into an accountable practice.
The orphan's property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity, a precise boundary against the taking-without-rida evoked by the section's definition of qahr.
The same ban on approaching orphan property except in the best way, followed by the demand to fulfill covenants, gives the section's emotional ethic a concrete legal edge.

Allah preserves a treasure under the wall for two orphan boys until they reach maturity, explicitly calling this their Lord's mercy; divine shelter protects both vulnerable children and their property.
Reform is named as the right purpose in handling orphans, who are called brothers; the ayah replaces domination with relational care while warning that Allah knows corrupter from reformer.
The believers who آوَوا and supported the emigrants turn shelter into a human act of loyalty, echoing divine shelter and the heart's compassionate turn in the section.
Those who believed, emigrated, sheltered, and supported are called true believers and promised provision, joining enacted refuge with a favorable divine response.
The Prophet is told that he will find no refuge apart from Allah; لَن تَجِدَ ... مُلْتَحَدًا brings the section's 'find' and 'shelter' motifs into one formulation.
The messenger declares that no one can protect him from Allah and that he will find no refuge apart from Him, again coupling finding with the direction of ultimate shelter.
Moses says that he hastened toward his Lord so that He might be pleased; movement, effort, and the sought direction of rida are explicit.
Guardians must not prevent former spouses from remarrying when they mutually agree honorably; تَرَاضَوْا بَيْنَهُم makes reciprocal rida a protection against coercive control.
After the required marital due, mutually agreed adjustment carries no blame; تَرَاضَيْتُم makes consent, effort, and material giving a two-sided relation.

Allah does not approve disbelief for His servants but approves gratitude for them; rida is aimed at a response rather than indiscriminately at persons, paralleling Lot's hatred of deeds rather than people.
They follow what angers Allah and hate His رضوان, placing divine anger and satisfaction at opposed ends and showing a heart deliberately oriented away from the pleasing end.
The ayah asks whether one who follows Allah's pleasure can be like one who incurs His anger, giving the lexicon's rida-versus-sakhat opposition an explicit moral form.
The Prophet is corrected for prohibiting what Allah made lawful while seeking his wives' satisfaction; human rida is a real aim but has a revealed boundary.

Hypocrites seek the believers' satisfaction by oaths, yet even human satisfaction cannot make Allah pleased with defiantly disobedient people; it breaks false assumed reciprocity between the two directions of rida.

The Prophet is warned that other communities will never be satisfied with him until he follows their way; satisfaction here exerts directional pressure, and revelation sets a boundary against yielding to it.
أَرَضِيتُم بِالْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا مِنَ الْآخِرَةِ rebukes satisfaction directed to the nearer life over the hereafter, reversing the surah's claim that the latter is better than the former.
Those pleased and settled with the worldly life direct rida toward what passes, illuminating by reversal the promised satisfaction attached to what Allah gives.
They are content to remain with those left behind and their hearts are sealed; rida becomes a chosen lowering of action rather than the fruitful response to divine giving.
Those with means nevertheless consent to remain behind and lose understanding through sealed hearts, another instance of satisfaction aimed at moral retreat.
The accusation that they do not honor the orphan is the behavioral opposite of a heart softened by having received divine care.
Greedily consuming inheritance enacts the taking-from-the-vulnerable without their rida that the section draws out of the prohibition of qahr.
Excessive love of wealth explains the misdirected heart behind the preceding neglect and consumption of the orphan's due.
Violently repelling the orphan is the direct enacted opposite of āwā as shelter and tender heartward return.
The prohibition on inheriting women against their will or constraining them to recover gifts precisely opposes acquisition without the other person's rida.
Allah alone is الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ; divine irresistible sovereignty marks the boundary around the human command not to use qahr against an orphan.
The repeated title الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ places qahr at the level of divine rule and guardianship, not a license for a powerful human over the vulnerable.
Joseph contrasts scattered lords with Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ, locating irresistible mastery in the one God while he speaks from unjust human confinement.
After denying that alleged partners create anything, the ayah names Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ; qahr belongs to the sole Creator, sharpening the limit on human overpowering.
All creation emerges before Allah الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ on the transformed earth, giving qahr its eschatological divine scale rather than the petty domination of an orphan.
The warning that there is no god but Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ makes overpowering an attribute of unique divinity, against which the human prohibition becomes legible.
In rejecting any divine child, the ayah names Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ; absolute qahr is paired with divine uniqueness, not human possession of another.
On the day all are exposed, dominion is declared to belong to Allah الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ, the ultimate boundary for every human claim to coercive mastery.
This neighbour identifies the promised recipient of 92:21 as one who gives his wealth to purify himself, letting the near-identical satisfaction promise be read as the result of a prior gift.
The giver seeks only the face of his Lord Most High; this specifies the upward direction of the effort that culminates in وَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ.
Selling oneself while seeking Allah's pleasure is an extreme instance of rida pursued through effort and directed toward God, rather than a mood that simply arrives.
Spending wealth in pursuit of Allah's pleasure and inner firmness connects effort, giving, and a heart-set direction to rida.
Charity, recognized good, and reconciliation become greatly rewarded when done seeking Allah's pleasure, showing concrete labor undertaken to attain rida.
The dispossessed emigrants seek bounty and pleasure from Allah after losing homes and property; hardship and active fidelity orient them toward divine rida.
Allah guides those who follow His pleasure into paths of peace, making rida an orientation that produces guidance and movement out of darkness.
Allah will admit the emigrants and slain believers into an entrance they will approve, another future divine giving whose result is their satisfaction.
A face in the hereafter is satisfied with its striving, linking completed effort to a later state of rida.
عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ turns the r-d-w root into the quality of the rewarded life itself, a secondary usage that makes promised satisfaction an encompassing condition.
The one whose scales are heavy enters عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ; rida-language again names the life granted after measured deeds.
The youths take refuge in the cave and ask their Lord for mercy and rightly prepared affairs, joining self-sought shelter to divine tenderness.
Allah shelters Mary and Jesus on secure high ground with flowing water, extending āwā to protection of a vulnerable mother and child.
Joseph takes his parents into his care and tells the family to enter Egypt in safety; reunion gives the root's sheltering act an affectionate family direction.

Moses's mother is told to nurse him, cast him into the river when afraid, and neither fear nor grieve because he will be returned; this sets the emotional peril answered by the love and shelter of 20:39.
The mother's heart becomes empty and is then bound firm by Allah, making divine action upon a distressed heart part of the infant-refuge scene.
Moses is prevented from accepting other nurses until his sister directs the household back toward his own family, the immediate means by which grief will turn into relief.
Jacob turns away in grief for Joseph until his eyes whiten, giving the section's dictionary statement that wajd can be grief a fully developed Quranic heart-scene.
Jacob says he finds Joseph's scent before the reunion; وَجَدَ here is sensory, yet the finding is inseparable in context from the enduring love and grief developed around Joseph.
Allah brings a people whom He loves and who love Him, a reciprocal love relation that parallels the reciprocal rida formula while directing their stance differently toward believers and rejecters.
The Merciful will appoint affection for those who believe and act rightly, another direct instance of love being divinely placed rather than self-generated.
They feed the needy, the orphan, and the captive despite love of the food, turning the heart's governing love into care for vulnerable recipients.
The feeders seek only Allah's face and want neither recompense nor thanks, specifying the direction of the love-driven orphan care in 76:8.
The ruling on orphan girls condemns withholding what is prescribed for them while desiring marriage and commands justice for vulnerable children, exposing how desire must be bounded by their rights.
After gardens and lasting dwellings are promised, Allah's rida is called greater; the emotional relation exceeds the gifts that accompany it even while those gifts lead into it.
The passing competition of worldly life is set against forgiveness and رضوان from Allah, placing enduring rida beyond what withers and sharpening the surah's latter-over-former horizon.
The believers are rebuked for casting affection toward active enemies; it is the negative counterpart to 60:7 and makes the proper object and direction of love the issue.
A building founded on reverence and Allah's pleasure is contrasted with one founded on a crumbling brink, turning rida into the intended ground of effort and exposing its destructive opposite.
Allah promises to exchange the believers' fear for security and establish for them the religion He has approved, joining divine rida, shelter-like security, and a bestowed change of state.
A polytheist who seeks protection must be sheltered and then conveyed to safety; compassion and refuge are required even toward someone outside the community and potential hostility.
Hatred of a people must not turn the believers away from justice; this directly bounds how loathing may be directed and what conduct may follow from it.
Later believers ask Allah to remove rancor from their hearts toward believers, making the removal of a hostile feeling from the heart an explicit divine gift.
Allah removes all rancor from the garden-dwellers' breasts and seats them as brothers facing one another, so cleared hostility becomes reciprocal nearness.
Allah removes rancor from the garden-dwellers' breasts as they acknowledge that divine guidance brought them to the granted garden, linking inward cleansing with received reward.
Allah removes rage from believers' hearts and turns mercifully toward whom He wills, a direct divinely caused alteration of the heart's hostile state.
The God-conscious restrain anger and pardon people, converting a strong hostile feeling into merciful conduct toward its possible object.

Pharaoh's household picks up Moses even though he will become an enemy and grief to them; this supplies the paradoxical hostile setting in which the love described in 20:39 moves Pharaoh's wife to protect him in 28:9.
Moses finds two women holding back their flock, recognizes their vulnerable position, and asks about it; an ordinary وَجَدَ immediately opens into attentive concern for others.
Moses waters for the women and then turns to his Lord in need, completing the compassionate action prompted by the finding in 28:23.
Failure to urge one another to feed the poor continues the orphan-neglect scene and identifies the absence of shared compassionate action between 89:17 and the greedy taking in 89:19.
Refusal to encourage feeding the poor continues the repulsion of the orphan in 107:2, showing that a hard heart withholds both personal shelter and communal concern.
Consuming orphan wealth unjustly is described as consuming fire, stating the consequence of the taking-without-rida that the section draws from qahr.
Fear of failing to act justly toward orphan girls changes what marriages are permitted, so adult desire is explicitly bounded by the vulnerable orphan's right to justice.

When orphans and other vulnerable people attend an estate division, they must be provided from it and addressed kindly; property distribution is joined to tender speech rather than overpowering exclusion.
Feeding an orphaned relative on a day of hunger gives a concrete positive form to the compassionate turn toward an orphan.
True righteousness includes giving cherished wealth to orphans and other vulnerable people, making love of possession yield to material care.
The one compelled outwardly while the heart remains secure in faith is excepted from blame, sharply distinguishing coerced action from the heart's actual willing direction.
The prohibition on compelling women into prostitution when they desire chastity is a precise boundary against exploiting another without her rida for material gain.
The same prophetic addressee is told to direct his longing toward his Lord, an explicit command for the heart's orientation after remembered divine gifts.

Jacob says that he complains his anguish and grief only to Allah; this clarifies the grief that surrounds his sensory 'finding' of Joseph's scent in 12:94 and gives the source dictionary's grief sense a named direction.
People may hate what is good for them and love what is bad for them, a direct warning that emotional direction does not by itself establish the worth of its object.
Love of Allah is tested by following the Prophet, after which Allah loves and forgives, giving love an enacted route and a reciprocal answer.
Those who avoid grave sins forgive when angered, showing the anger face of the heart governed into merciful action rather than coercion.
The covenant joins worship of Allah with good conduct toward orphans and other dependents, placing care for the orphan inside a binding relational duty.
Kind treatment of orphans is included among the concrete human relations that must follow exclusive worship, extending received divine care into care of dependents.
The declaration that there is no compulsion in religion supplies a broad but explicit boundary between coerced submission and willing heart-direction.
Lot wishes he had strength against the crowd or could take refuge in a powerful support, using the āwā root for sought protection in a scene of exposed vulnerability.
The command to labor when free supplies the exertion immediately before the heartward direction of 94:8, paralleling the section's claim that rida is brought through effort.
Allah gives believers glad tidings of mercy, satisfaction, and lasting gardens, presenting divine rida together with promised gifts to their recipients.
Gardens, purified spouses, and Allah's satisfaction are offered as what is better than worldly desires, joining bestowed reward with rida and the latter-over-former contrast.
The believers follow Allah's pleasure after fear and return with bounty untouched by harm, making rida the chosen direction of a difficult response.
Pilgrims are described as seeking bounty and satisfaction from their Lord, another concrete pairing of active pursuit, divine giving, and rida.
The Prophet's companions seek bounty and satisfaction from Allah, with the marks of sustained worship visible on them; effort is directed toward divine rida.
Allah says that He has approved Islam as religion for the believers, using rida as divine acceptance directed toward a way rather than as affection indiscriminately directed toward persons.
